growth_story.headline: Kazakhstan's income per person collapsed in the 1990s, grew 8.9 percent a year with oil to 2007, and has grown 2.5 percent a year since 2008.
growth_story.arc: Income per person fell 4.6 percent a year from 1991 to 1998, as output and exports collapsed after the Soviet Union broke up and inflation ran out of control. From 1999 to 2007 it grew 8.9 percent a year as oil production rose and world commodity prices climbed, and in 2003 it passed its 1990 level. Since 2008 growth has averaged 2.5 percent a year: it stopped in 2009 during the global financial crisis, picked up again, and turned to small declines in 2015 and 2016 after the 2014 fall in commodity prices. Over the last decade (2016 to 2025) it averaged 2.1 percent a year, against 4.2 in the decade before, and that decade included a fall of 3.9 percent in 2020. In 2025 rising oil output and strong spending at home lifted income per person by 5.2 percent. That took it to its highest level so far, about 12,492 in constant dollars.

threads.title: Collapse after independence
threads.text: After 1991 the economy's production ties with the other former Soviet republics were cut. Output and exports fell steeply, and inflation peaked in 1994. This is why income per person shrank 4.6 percent a year from 1991 to 1998.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 rising oil output and strong spending at home pushed growth up, and income per person grew 5.2 percent, its fastest since 2011. By the first half of 2026 growth had eased, because oil production fell during field maintenance and disruption on export routes, and inflation stayed above the central bank's target.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person up 5.2 percent in 2025 to a new high, and the sources describe a strong, oil-led year. Yet the World Bank's Macro Poverty Outlook (October 2026) reports that households' real incomes shrank during 2025, barely grew in early 2026, and real wages were falling. The rise in output per person was not matched by household incomes.
